newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Activists fight to keep ban on ivory trade.
newsitem.headline: Activists fight to keep ban on ivory trade.

text.p: Allowing resumed trade in ivory would be the world's biggest conservation blunder, green activists fighting to ensure the survival of wild elephants said on Monday.
Trade in ivory is banned under terms of an international convention but several southern African countries want the embargo lifted.
Activists meeting in Johannesburg to plan a united strategy against the proposal said it would reverse the restoration of elephant populations wiped out in many areas.

"The proposals risk a massive increase in elephant poaching across Africa and Asia and threaten the successful recovery of elephant populations," the Environmental Investigation Agency said in a statement released at the start of the conference.
The seven-year-old ban has been a big success and populations of the once-endangered animals have rebounded.
Botswana, Namibia and Zimbabwe plan to petition a meeting of the 134-member Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES) in Harare next month to allow resumed trade.
They hope to convince the convention that the ban merely drives trade underground, and propose that ivory collected from periodic culls to keep numbers down be auctioned under tight controls instead.

"If accepted, these proposals would be the biggest conservation blunder of the century, from which elephants in range states will never recover," Perez Olindo, director of the African Elephant Foundation International, said in a statement.
South Africa, Namibia, Zimbabwe and Mozambique all have large elephant populations and ivory from the purges has been stockpiled since the ban.
Botswana says its 30-tonne ivory stockpile is the result of natural deaths and seizures from poachers and illegal traders. Officials say they have a Japanese buyer for the ivory.
A similar move by Botswana in 1992, involving another buyer, was voted down.
South African conservation officials recently had to abandon an effort to slow elephant population growth by using hormonal birth control.
Instead of ensuring the elephant cows were not able to conceive, the "pill" put them in a state of continuous oestrus.
